evidence.quoted_text:
"manager_restarted": (
            (((manager.get("before") or {}).get("manager") or {})
             .get("pid") or 0) > 0
            and (((manager.get("after") or {}).get("manager") or {})
                 .get("pid") or 0) > 0
            and (manager.get("before") or {}).get("manager", {}).get("pid")
            != (manager.get("after") or {}).get("manager", {}).get("pid")
            and bool(((manager.get("before") or {}).get("manager") or {})
                     .get("invocation_id"))
            and bool(((manager.get("after") or {}).get("manager") or {})
                     .get("invocation_id"))
            and (manager.get("before") or {}).get("manager", {}).get("invocation_id")
            != (manager.get("after") or {}).get("manager", {}).get("invocation_id")),
evidence.reason: The `manager_restarted` predicate (lines 1104-1116) checks only that the before/after manager PID and invocation ID are nonempty and differ. It never compares the boot IDs of the two manager snapshots, even though the snapshot evidence includes `boot_id` and the reboot step separately guards its own snapshots in `boot_id_changed` (lines 1117-1124). A guest reboot between the restart command and the second inspect yields different PIDs and invocation IDs on the new boot, so `manager_restarted` passes without an isolated manager restart, and `mask_persisted` can then rely on reboot-contaminated observations; the later planned reboot still satisfies its own boot-ID check. Adding nonempty, equal boot IDs to the manager snapshot pair while retaining the PID and invocation-ID checks is the smallest fix for this false acceptance.
